title: Google-first SWE Interview Lab
notice: This is an original practice bank based on enduring software-engineering interview patterns. It is not an archive of Google's confidential or verbatim interview questions, and it does not claim a question appeared in a particular year.

items.question: Given an integer array and a target, return the indices of two distinct values that sum to the target.
items.answer: Scan once while storing each value's index in a hash map. For each value x, check whether target - x is already present; if so return the saved index and current index. Insert x only after checking so one element cannot be reused. Expected O(n) time and O(n) space.
items.followups: What if multiple answers exist? What if the input is sorted? What if values repeat?
items.complexity: O(n) expected time, O(n) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
items.answer: Maintain a left boundary and a map from each character to its latest index. When a repeated character lies inside the current window, move left to max(left, lastSeen + 1). Update the last-seen index and the maximum window length on each step. State whether indexing is by UTF-16 code unit, Unicode code point, or byte.
items.followups: Why is max(left, lastSeen + 1) necessary? How do Unicode characters affect the implementation?
items.complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space for the character set
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Search for a target in a sorted array and return its index, or -1 if absent.
items.answer: Use a half-open interval [left, right). While left < right, compute mid = left + (right - left) / 2. If a[mid] < target, set left = mid + 1; otherwise set right = mid. After convergence, check left < n and a[left] == target. Explain the invariant and avoid overflow in midpoint arithmetic.
items.followups: How would you find the first occurrence among duplicates? What changes for a rotated sorted array?
items.complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Merge a list of overlapping time intervals.
items.answer: Sort intervals by start time. Append the first interval, then compare each next interval with the last merged interval. If they overlap, extend the end to the maximum end; otherwise append a new interval. Clarify whether touching endpoints count as overlap.
items.followups: What if input is already sorted? How would you insert one interval into a sorted non-overlapping list?
items.complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting, O(n) output space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.
items.answer: Keep a main stack and a min stack. Push onto min stack when the value is less than or equal to its current top; pop from min stack when the popped value equals its top. Using <= correctly handles duplicate minima. Alternatively store value/minimum pairs.
items.followups: How do duplicates affect the min stack? Can you do it with one stack and encoded values?
items.complexity: O(1) per operation, O(n) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Reverse a singly linked list in place.
items.answer: Track prev=null, current=head. On each iteration save next=current.next, point current.next to prev, then advance prev=current and current=next. Return prev. Draw pointer changes for empty, one-node, and multi-node lists.
items.followups: Can you do it recursively? How do you reverse nodes in groups of k?
items.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space iteratively
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Validate whether a binary tree is a binary search tree.
items.answer: Recurse with exclusive lower and upper bounds. A node must satisfy lower < value < upper; its left subtree inherits the upper bound as the node value and its right subtree inherits the lower bound. This catches invalid descendants that parent-only comparisons miss. Clarify duplicate-key policy.
items.followups: How would you validate a BST iteratively? What if duplicate values are permitted on one side?
items.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree.
items.answer: Use a queue initialized with the root. For each level, capture the queue size, pop exactly that many nodes, append their values, and enqueue non-null children. The size snapshot keeps levels separated.
items.followups: How would you return the right-side view? What is the memory bound for a wide tree?
items.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) queue space where w is maximum width
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Count connected islands in a grid of land and water cells.
items.answer: Scan every cell. On each unvisited land cell, increment the count and run DFS/BFS to mark all connected land as visited. Choose four-way or eight-way adjacency explicitly. Mutating the grid avoids a separate visited matrix if allowed.
items.followups: What if the grid is too large for recursion? How would you parallelize safely?
items.complexity: O(rows × columns) time, O(rows × columns) worst-case auxiliary space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Given course prerequisites, determine whether all courses can be completed.
items.answer: Model courses as a directed graph. Kahn's algorithm computes indegrees, queues every zero-indegree node, repeatedly removes one and decrements its neighbors. If the processed count equals the number of vertices, there is no cycle; otherwise a cycle blocks completion. DFS coloring is an alternative.
items.followups: How do you return one valid order? How would you report a cycle?
items.complexity: O(V + E) time and space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Find the kth largest element in an unsorted array.
items.answer: Maintain a min-heap of size k: insert each number and remove the minimum when size exceeds k. The heap top is the kth largest. Discuss quickselect for expected linear time and sorting when simplicity matters.
items.followups: When does quickselect degrade? How would you process a stream?
items.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space for heap approach
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Given coin denominations and an amount, find the minimum number of coins or report impossible.
items.answer: Define dp[x] as the minimum coins for amount x. Set dp[0]=0 and other entries to infinity. For each amount x, try every coin c <= x and update dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x-c]+1) when the prior state is reachable. Return impossible if dp[amount] remains infinity.
items.followups: Why does greedy fail for arbitrary denominations? How would you count combinations instead of minimizing coins?
items.complexity: O(amount × number of denominations) time, O(amount) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Determine whether a string can be segmented into words from a dictionary.
items.answer: Let dp[i] mean the prefix ending before index i can be segmented. Set dp[0]=true. For each reachable end i, test dictionary words that could end there and set dp[i] if the preceding prefix is reachable. A trie or maximum word length can reduce unnecessary checks.
items.followups: How would you return one segmentation? What changes if dictionary lookups are expensive?
items.complexity: Typical O(n²) transitions with constant-time dictionary lookup; O(n) DP space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design an LRU cache with get and put operations in O(1) expected time.
items.answer: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered most-recent to least-recent. A successful get moves its node to the front. Put updates existing nodes or inserts a new node; if capacity is exceeded, remove the tail node and its map entry. Use sentinel nodes to simplify pointer handling.
items.followups: How do you make it thread-safe? What if entries have TTLs? What metrics would you expose?
items.complexity: O(1) expected per operation, O(capacity) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Implement a thread-safe in-memory counter in Java and explain the trade-offs between synchronized and AtomicLong.
items.answer: For a simple counter use AtomicLong.incrementAndGet for atomic increments and get for reads. It is suitable when operations are independent atomic updates. synchronized is useful when a compound invariant spans several fields or operations. Define required visibility, ordering, overflow behavior, and expected contention before choosing.
items.followups: When would LongAdder be preferable? How do you test races? What does linearizability mean here?
items.complexity: Atomic operation is constant-time conceptually; contention and throughput depend on workload
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design an idempotent POST API for creating a payment or order when clients may retry after timeouts.
items.answer: Require an idempotency key scoped to the caller and operation. Persist the key, request fingerprint, status, and result under a uniqueness constraint. In one transaction, claim the key and create the operation; duplicates with the same fingerprint return the stored result, while key reuse with a different payload returns a conflict. Define retention and in-progress behavior.
items.followups: What happens if the process crashes after charging but before storing success? How do downstream providers support idempotency?
items.complexity: Database and external-call costs dominate; uniqueness and transaction boundaries enforce correctness
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: A service processes the same queue message more than once. How would you prevent duplicate business effects?
items.answer: Assume at-least-once delivery unless the broker guarantees otherwise. Use a stable event ID and an inbox/deduplication table with a uniqueness constraint, and commit deduplication plus the business mutation atomically. Make downstream side effects idempotent or publish via an outbox. Retain deduplication records for the replay horizon.
items.followups: Why is a distributed lock not always enough? How do poison messages and retries work?
items.complexity: Depends on storage and throughput; correctness hinges on atomic persistence and idempotency
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a URL-shortening service for high read volume and global traffic.
items.answer: Clarify scale, latency, custom aliases, expiry, privacy, and analytics. Write API creates a code and stores code→URL; redirect API checks cache then storage. Use collision-safe ID generation or retry on unique constraint, replicated storage, regional caches, abuse detection, rate limits, and async analytics. Discuss cache invalidation, hot keys, availability, and redirect semantics.
items.followups: Estimate QPS and storage. How do you handle deletion, malicious URLs, and a viral hot link?
items.complexity: State assumptions and bottlenecks; separate read path from analytics writes
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a distributed rate limiter for APIs used across multiple application instances.
items.answer: Clarify limits, identity, burst behavior, and acceptable clock error. Token bucket supports bursts with an average rate; a shared atomic store or partitioned limiter coordinates instances. Define key cardinality, TTL, hot-key strategy, and fail-open/closed policy. Return limit headers and monitor rejects, latency, and store failures.
items.followups: Compare fixed window, sliding log, sliding counter, and token bucket. What if the limiter store is down?
items.complexity: Per-request work should be bounded; coordination latency and key distribution dominate
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a notification platform for email, SMS, and push with retries and user preferences.
items.answer: Accept an idempotent request, validate preferences and templates, persist intent, and publish through an outbox to queues. Provider workers use bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, provider-specific rate limits, and dead-letter handling. Track status, suppress duplicates, honor unsubscribe/quiet hours, and expose delivery metrics.
items.followups: How do you order notifications? How do you avoid retry storms? What is the delivery guarantee?
items.complexity: Asynchronous throughput scales with workers; durability and provider quotas constrain capacity
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a metrics ingestion and alerting pipeline for millions of time series.
items.answer: Separate ingestion, buffering, aggregation, storage, query, and alert evaluation. Partition by tenant and series identity, batch writes, apply backpressure, and define retention/downsampling. Control cardinality, protect noisy tenants, and evaluate alerts with clear window and missing-data semantics. Include replication, recovery, and cost controls.
items.followups: How do you prevent cardinality explosions? How do you deliver alerts once or at least once?
items.complexity: Estimate samples per second and bytes per sample; identify ingestion and query bottlenecks
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Design a file upload service for large files with resumability and malware scanning.
items.answer: Use an authenticated API to create an upload session and issue short-lived signed object-storage URLs. Upload in chunks with checksums and resumable state. Finalization verifies size and hashes, emits an event for malware scanning, and only then marks the object available. Enforce quotas, expiry, access controls, and lifecycle cleanup.
items.followups: How do you prevent users from reading unscanned files? What if finalization is retried?
items.complexity: Object storage handles bytes; metadata, state transitions, and security gates need strong correctness
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Tell me about a production incident you helped resolve. What did you do and what changed afterward?
items.answer: Use a truthful STAR response: Situation and customer/business impact; Task and your ownership; Actions with specific diagnosis, collaboration, mitigation, and trade-offs; Result with measurable outcome; Learning with a prevention step. Separate your contribution from the team's work and avoid inventing metrics.
items.followups: What would you do differently? How did you communicate uncertainty? What permanent fix reduced recurrence?
items.complexity: Score clarity, ownership, evidence, collaboration, and learning on a 1–5 rubric
items.source: Original behavioral practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Describe a time you disagreed with a technical decision. How did you reach an outcome?
items.answer: Choose a real disagreement. Explain the shared goal, constraints, alternatives, evidence you gathered, how you listened and communicated risk, the decision process, and the outcome. Show that you can commit to a decision after discussion and learn from the result.
items.followups: What if your preferred approach lost? How did you keep the relationship productive?
items.complexity: Score evidence, empathy, judgment, collaboration, and outcome on a 1–5 rubric
items.source: Original behavioral practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: Tell me about a project where requirements were ambiguous and you had to make progress.
items.answer: Describe how you identified unknowns, separated reversible from irreversible decisions, asked targeted questions, proposed a small measurable milestone, validated assumptions with stakeholders, and adapted when evidence changed. Include real outcomes and what you would improve.
items.followups: How did you decide what not to build? How did you communicate risks and changing scope?
items.complexity: Score problem framing, prioritization, communication, adaptability, and impact on a 1–5 rubric
items.source: Original interview-style practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: A production endpoint's p95 latency doubled after a release, but average latency barely changed. How would you investigate?
items.answer: Confirm metric definitions and compare by route, region, version, dependency, and request size. Inspect traces and p50/p95/p99, errors, saturation, queue depth, and database plans. Compare release diffs and feature flags; mitigate via rollback or disabling the suspected path while preserving evidence. Add a regression test and guardrail after root cause is confirmed.
items.followups: Why can averages hide tail latency? How do you distinguish a slow dependency from lock contention?
items.complexity: Use a hypothesis-driven investigation and define rollback criteria
items.source: Original interview-style practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: How would you test a method that parses and validates a complex request payload?
items.answer: Cover valid minimal and maximal payloads, missing fields, nulls, type errors, boundary values, malformed encodings, duplicate fields, and security-relevant input. Use table-driven unit tests, property-based tests for invariants, contract tests for API shape, and integration tests for persistence. Assert error codes and avoid brittle assertions on incidental messages.
items.followups: Which tests belong at unit vs integration level? How do you prevent test data from leaking secrets?
items.complexity: Aim for meaningful branch and boundary coverage rather than a raw percentage
items.source: Original interview-style practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.

items.question: You need the median of a stream of integers after every insertion. Design the data structure.
items.answer: Maintain a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Keep sizes equal or lower half one larger, and ensure max(lower) <= min(upper). Insert based on the lower heap top, rebalance, then return the top or average of both tops. Define overflow-safe averaging for integer types.
items.followups: How do you support deletion? What if values arrive from multiple partitions?
items.complexity: O(log n) insertion, O(1) median lookup, O(n) space
items.source: Original practice prompt; not represented as a verbatim historical Google question.
